section_summary: This section documents mounting public and congressional pressure for broader restrictions on exports of oil, gasoline, scrap metal, and other war materials to Japan, together with State Department explanations of the developing export-control system. It also contains extensive material on Universal Oil Products’ petroleum-technology contracts and litigation with Japan Gasoline Company, including an amended federal complaint alleging that the American company stopped performance because of the State Department’s “moral embargo.” The final portion covers British-American coordination over Japanese oil supplies, Japanese purchasing inquiries, reported gasoline shipments, and Anglo-Dutch oil negotiations in Asia.

subfiles.title: Allen T. Treadway letter forwarding Gertrude Allen’s protest
subfiles.about: Forwards a constituent’s question about American sales of oil and scrap iron to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Treadway quotes Gertrude Allen’s characterization of the trade as “infamous” and asks the Secretary of State for an explanation. The letter initiates a short congressional-constituent exchange concerning controls on strategic exports.

subfiles.title: Cordell Hull reply to Allen T. Treadway
subfiles.about: Explains the proclamations and regulations governing exports of petroleum products, scrap metal, and aviation-fuel technology.
subfiles.summary: Hull cites the Export Control Act and the presidential controls announced in July and September 1940. He notes additional restrictions on aviation gasoline, iron and steel scrap, equipment for producing aviation fuel or tetraethyl lead, and associated technical documentation, enclosing copies of the relevant measures.

subfiles.title: Tokyo telegram on Japanese reaction to the American scrap embargo
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese press and industrial reactions to the announced American embargo on iron and steel scrap.
subfiles.summary: Japanese newspapers uniformly portrayed the measure as aimed at Japan, while minimizing its immediate economic effect and predicting revisions to industrial steel allocations. The Yomiuri expected an eventual oil embargo to bring relations near the breaking point but argued that Japan could pursue a self-sufficient East Asian economy using domestic, Chinese, Indochinese, South Seas, and North Sakhalin resources plus German and Italian assistance.

subfiles.title: Senate referral of Ralph S. Binns’s inquiry
subfiles.about: Refers Ralph S. Binns’s questions about restrictions on exports to Japan to the State Department.
subfiles.summary: The brief Senate communication transmits the matter for departmental attention. It serves as the cover for Binns’s attached September 30 letter.

subfiles.title: Ralph S. Binns letter to Arthur H. Vandenberg
subfiles.about: Asks whether export controls leave Japan free to buy unrestricted grades of oil and scrap iron and where company-level export information can be found.
subfiles.summary: Binns says he has heard that gasoline, oil, and proposed scrap restrictions cover only specified grades. He also asks for a source identifying which oil companies continue to sell gasoline and oil to Japan.

subfiles.title: State Department cover reply to Arthur H. Vandenberg
subfiles.about: Returns Binns’s letter and encloses a copy of the Department’s substantive reply.
subfiles.summary: The Department acknowledges Vandenberg’s October 2 referral. It returns the original constituent letter together with its response to Ralph S. Binns.

subfiles.title: Charles W. Yost reply to Ralph S. Binns
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Clarifies the scope of restrictions on scrap iron, aviation gasoline, and confidential export-license information.
subfiles.summary: Yost explains that scrap licenses would be issued only for the Western Hemisphere and Great Britain and that gasoline controls applied to fuel meeting the regulatory definition of aviation motor fuel. He declines to identify companies from confidential license applications but directs Binns to the Commerce Department’s aggregate export statistics.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note for Warren A. Seavey letter
subfiles.about: Redirects researchers to the original Warren A. Seavey letter on shipments of war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The sheet identifies the subject as the shipment of war materials to Japan. It states that the original September 24 letter is filed under decimal number 893.51/7146.

subfiles.title: Pat Cannon letter protesting a Palm Beach scrap shipment
subfiles.about: Urges immediate action to stop a ship at Palm Beach from loading scrap iron for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cannon reports that the American Legion in West Palm Beach strongly opposes the shipment. Although he recognizes that the new restriction will not take effect until later in October, he asks the Department to find a means of stopping this and other exports of strategic materials to unfriendly countries.

subfiles.title: Cordell Hull reply to Pat Cannon
subfiles.about: Explains the effective dates and terms of the new controls on iron and steel scrap exports.
subfiles.summary: Hull states that existing licenses would be cancelled on October 16 and that all grades of iron and steel scrap would then require licenses. He adds that licenses would be issued only for the Western Hemisphere and Great Britain and encloses the White House release and implementing customs instruction.

subfiles.title: Universal Oil Products application letter concerning Japan Gasoline Company
subfiles.from: H. J. Halle, Universal Oil Products Company
subfiles.about: Submits license applications for technical plans and documents useful in producing aviation motor fuel in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Universal Oil Products says Japan Gasoline Company has requested plans and specifications under existing agreements. It describes technical material already supplied for a Mitsui Mining pyrolytic cracking and clay-treating plant processing Kogasin products and asks for export licenses under the September proclamation.

subfiles.title: L. M. Healy letter enclosing the Japan Gasoline amended complaint
subfiles.from: L. M. Healy, Universal Oil Products Company
subfiles.about: Transmits an amended federal complaint and an oil-industry item on a proposed Korean isooctane plant.
subfiles.summary: Healy explains that the amended complaint seeks specific performance of the 1938 agreements plus two million dollars for delay, or ten million dollars as an alternative remedy. He also encloses an Oil & Gas Journal report about plans for an isooctane plant in Korea.

subfiles.title: “Korea to Have Isooctane Plant” industry extract
subfiles.about: Reports planned Korean and Japanese facilities for isooctane, antiknock agents, and tetraethyl lead.
subfiles.summary: The extract says Korean Oil Company planned an aviation-fuel isooctane plant while two Universal-designed plants were located at Kawasaki. It also reports Japanese projects at Kamata and elsewhere to produce ethylene dibromide and tetraethyl lead amid uncertainty over access to American engineering assistance.

subfiles.title: Japan Gasoline Company amended complaint against Universal Oil Products
subfiles.from: Nihon Kihatsuyu Kabushiki Kaisha (Japan Gasoline Company), through its attorneys
subfiles.to: United States District Court for the District of Delaware
subfiles.about: Seeks enforcement of petroleum-technology agreements and damages for Universal Oil Products’ refusal to continue performance.
subfiles.summary: The complaint traces the 1928 contract with Hisashi Sekiguchi, its assignment to Japan Gasoline Company, Universal’s corporate succession, and three 1938 memoranda granting rights in isooctane, hydrogenation, catalysts, and other petroleum processes. It alleges that Universal accepted substantial payments and orders for Japanese plants but withheld plans, engineers, patents, and technical information after December 1939, attributing its refusal to the State Department’s nonlegal “moral embargo.” The pleading requests specific performance plus two million dollars for delay, or alternatively ten million dollars in damages, along with continuing jurisdiction over future losses.

subfiles.title: Charles W. Yost acknowledgment to L. M. Healy
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of the amended complaint and the report on a Korean isooctane plant.
subfiles.summary: Yost records that the complaint concerns the 1938 agreements rather than the 1928 contract. He repeats the requested remedies of specific performance with two million dollars for delay or ten million dollars in alternative damages.

subfiles.title: Lindley Beckworth transmittal of John H. Woodard’s letter
subfiles.about: Forwards John H. Woodard’s letter concerning exports to Japan for State Department consideration.
subfiles.summary: The surviving page is largely congressional letterhead and filing notation. The Department’s later response identifies it as Beckworth’s October 8 referral of Woodard’s letter.

subfiles.title: John H. Woodard letter criticizing trade with Japan
subfiles.about: Demands an explanation for continued American exports of pig iron, petroleum, gasoline, and oil to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Woodard argues that Japan uses American supplies to wage war in China while aligning itself with Germany and Italy and intimidating the United States. He contends that public opinion favors firmer resistance and asks Beckworth to obtain an explanation of the government’s policy.

subfiles.title: Cordell Hull reply to Lindley Beckworth
subfiles.about: Provides export-control proclamations and press releases for John H. Woodard’s information.
subfiles.summary: Hull lists the July, September, and September 30 proclamations issued under the Export Control Act and the White House announcements restricting aviation gasoline and scrap exports. He adds that the interested government departments continue to consider further controls and returns Woodard’s letter.

subfiles.title: John E. Rankin letter forwarding Romayne Berryman’s appeal
subfiles.about: Requests attention and a report on Romayne Berryman’s letter advocating stronger action toward Japan.
subfiles.summary: Rankin asks the Secretary to consider the attached constituent communication. He also requests that Berryman’s letter be returned for his files after the Department replies.

subfiles.title: Romayne Berryman letter advocating a wider embargo
subfiles.about: Urges an embargo on all war materials and motor fuel rather than scrap iron alone.
subfiles.summary: Berryman describes American policy toward Japan as insufficiently strong and calls the scrap restriction largely symbolic because Japan had already accumulated supplies. She asks Rankin to use his influence in support of broader action.

subfiles.title: Cordell Hull reply to John E. Rankin
subfiles.about: Summarizes existing export controls and supplies explanatory documents for Romayne Berryman.
subfiles.summary: Hull cites the Export Control Act proclamations and White House releases restricting aviation gasoline and iron and steel scrap to approved destinations. He says the government continues to examine the question of additional controls and returns Berryman’s letter.

subfiles.title: Secretary’s routing slip to Maxwell M. Hamilton
subfiles.from: Office of the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Refers the following correspondence to Hamilton for reply.
subfiles.summary: The brief departmental sheet contains only an instruction that Mr. Hamilton prepare the response. It precedes Egbert W. Smith’s letter concerning American aid to Japan.

subfiles.title: Egbert W. Smith letter opposing supplies to Japan
subfiles.about: Asks why the United States continues furnishing Japan with war supplies used against China.
subfiles.summary: Smith argues that American interests and public sentiment favor China and oppose assistance to Japan. He requests an explanation for what he regards as the government’s failure to stop supplies useful to Japanese aggression.

subfiles.title: Maxwell M. Hamilton reply to Egbert W. Smith
subfiles.from: Maxwell M. Hamilton, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains the moral embargo, the limited export of formal arms, and the national-defense basis of statutory export controls.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton says advisory action had largely stopped American deliveries of aircraft and aeronautical equipment to countries bombing civilian populations and that other formally defined arms shipments to Japan had been negligible. He stresses that controls under the July 1940 act were legally grounded in national defense and administered through the export-control system. He concludes that the Department was balancing Far Eastern conditions, American interests, law, and public opinion.

subfiles.title: Charles W. Yost memorandum of conversation with Universal Oil Products
subfiles.about: Records a discussion about whether Universal Oil Products could perform its 1938 contract with Japan Gasoline Company.
subfiles.summary: Halle and Healy asked whether they could supply polymerization and hydrogenation information requested by Saneyoshi. Yost confidentially advised that the government was considering a legal licensing basis for controls on plans and technical information used to produce aviation fuel, leading Halle to defer commitments. The participants also discussed the pending lawsuit, synthetic rubber, and toluene, with Halle stating that he would not seek permission to furnish Japan a process so clearly useful for war.

subfiles.title: Fragment of propaganda commentary on the American embargo
subfiles.about: Denounces American export restrictions as discriminatory measures directed at Japan and aligned with Britain, France, and China.
subfiles.summary: The fragment argues that American neutrality is fraudulent because the United States supplies Britain and France while restricting Japan. It portrays Germany and Japan as victorious builders of new orders in Europe and East Asia, dismisses Chiang Kai-shek as nearly defeated, and calls on Asian peoples to unite against the Western democracies.

subfiles.title: Division of Controls instruction concerning a press release
subfiles.about: Requests preparation of a letter enclosing the accompanying White House press release.
subfiles.summary: The handwritten note is an internal drafting instruction. It links the file correspondence to the September 26 release on iron and steel scrap controls.

subfiles.title: White House release on control of iron and steel scrap exports
subfiles.about: Announces comprehensive licensing controls on iron and steel scrap exports.
subfiles.summary: The President approved additional controls to conserve scrap for the expanding American defense program. Existing licenses for No. 1 heavy melting steel scrap would be revoked on October 15, and from October 16 licenses for all grades would be limited to shipments to the Western Hemisphere and Great Britain.

subfiles.title: J. Goux report on Associated Ethyl shipments
subfiles.to: Secretary of State, attention Charles W. Yost
subfiles.about: Reports that Associated Ethyl Company made no August shipments of ethyl fluid to Japan or Russia.
subfiles.summary: Goux supplies the requested monthly negative report. The letter confirms that neither Japan nor the Soviet Union received ethyl fluid from the company during August 1940.

subfiles.title: Charles W. Yost reply ending voluntary ethyl-fluid reports
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Thanks Goux for the report and states that further voluntary shipment reports are unnecessary under the new licensing regulations.
subfiles.summary: Yost notes that tetraethyl lead and ethyl fluid are now controlled by the July 26 proclamation and implementing regulations. He thanks the company for its cooperation and encloses copies of those measures.

subfiles.title: Joseph C. Green memorandum on the Japanese Embassy’s request
subfiles.about: Records Morito Morishima’s request for a formal answer to the Japanese ambassador’s July note about aviation-gasoline contracts.
subfiles.summary: Morishima said the Embassy had received no reply to Note No. 156 concerning American-Japanese contracts for plans and specifications for high-quality aviation gasoline. He requested a response chiefly as a formality and to complete the Embassy’s files, and Green agreed to investigate.

subfiles.title: State Department note to the Japanese ambassador
subfiles.about: Formally answers the ambassador’s July 9 note concerning the Universal Oil Products–Japan Gasoline contract.
subfiles.summary: The Department states that it had written Universal Oil Products on August 15. That letter expressed no objection to the companies’ arrangement for Universal to resume performance under their July 19, 1928 contract.

subfiles.title: Andrew Agnew letter enclosing a note on Far Eastern oil
subfiles.about: Requests Hornbeck’s comments and a meeting about an unofficial analysis of oil supplies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Agnew explains that he prepared the enclosed note for his own guidance and that it was neither official nor diplomatically worded. He asks whether Hornbeck agrees with its general conclusions and offers to discuss it at the State Department.

subfiles.title: “The Far East—Oil” policy note
subfiles.about: Analyzes the need for British-American coordination over oil supplies and economic pressure on Japan.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum argues that British, Dutch, and American oil policies must be coordinated to avoid mutual suspicion and Japanese exploitation of divergent policies. It reviews American restrictions, Japanese pressure on British-Dutch suppliers, negotiations at Yokohama and Batavia, Iranian supplies, and continuing deliveries from the United States, Saudi Arabia, Peru, and Ecuador. It urges advance consultation before further American action and a clearer mutual understanding of commitments that Britain and the Netherlands might be forced to make.

subfiles.title: Japanese Shell and Standard Vacuum oil inquiries
subfiles.to: British Embassy and State Department file
subfiles.about: Tabulates Japanese naval and planning-agency requests for crude oil, gasoline, aviation gasoline, kerosene, and diesel fuel.
subfiles.summary: The statement totals Shell-group and Standard Vacuum inquiries at more than 3.1 million tons per year. Its detailed continuation associates the requests with Yokohama cables and distinguishes Navy, Plans Department, quota, Miri, and Tarakan requirements.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Japanese crude-oil pricing and quantities
subfiles.about: Reviews a Japanese counteroffer for crude oil and explains estimated quantities in the attached inquiry summary.
subfiles.summary: The Plans Department proposed pricing Crude C against Kettleman Hills crude plus pipeline charges, producing a much lower figure than London’s offer once the Pacific freight premium was included. The writer explains uncertain Navy and planning-agency quantities and adds Standard Vacuum figures supplied by Mr. Walden.

subfiles.title: “Gasoline” list of recent shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: Lists recent gasoline and ethyl-fluid shipments to Japan and reports urgent additional Japanese orders.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum identifies ships, ports, sailing dates, and quantities moving mainly from Gulf Coast and California ports. It reports that Japanese buyers sought large additional deliveries by October 15 and notes that 73-octane base gasoline could be leaded to 86–87 octane while remaining outside the American aviation-gasoline definition if it stayed below 87 octane.

subfiles.title: “Gasoline for Japan” duplicate shipment report
subfiles.about: Provides a second copy of the report on heavy gasoline shipments and pending Japanese orders.
subfiles.summary: This version repeats the vessel-by-vessel record of gasoline and ethyl-fluid cargoes from American ports and the reported orders involving Cities Service, Republic, Taylor, Associated, Mitsui, Nissho, and Mitsubishi. It again emphasizes the unprecedented pace of shipments and the regulatory significance of gasoline just below the 87-octane threshold.

subfiles.title: George J. Bates letter forwarding Leo Alexander’s protest
subfiles.about: Forwards Leo Alexander’s letter and asks what the government is doing about exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Bates requests a report on the issues raised by Alexander. He also asks that the enclosed letter be returned after it has served the Department’s purpose.

subfiles.title: Leo Alexander letter advocating comprehensive sanctions
subfiles.about: Calls for an embargo on gasoline and all raw materials and for a complete halt to imports from Japan.
subfiles.summary: Alexander argues that the scrap-iron embargo is insufficient because Japan has openly become an American enemy. He proposes excluding Japanese silk from the American market both to damage Japan’s economy and to strengthen domestic nylon and rayon industries.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to George J. Bates
subfiles.about: Assures Bates that the Department and other agencies are studying the export-policy issues raised by Leo Alexander.
subfiles.summary: The Department says the problem and related questions are receiving careful interagency consideration. It promises action as circumstances warrant and returns Alexander’s letter as requested.

subfiles.title: G. S. Walden letter quoting cable instructions on Japanese oil negotiations
subfiles.about: Provides the text of an oil-company cable, previously cleared with Hornbeck, setting limits and terms for Japanese supply negotiations.
subfiles.summary: The cable instructs Yokohama negotiators to clarify the separate demands of the Japanese Navy, Plans Department, and Central authorities before considering further supplies. It renews offers for crude oil and one aviation-gasoline cargo but limits crude commitments to six months, requires acceptance by September 30, and specifies payment in U.S. dollars and guilders through New York and Batavia.

subfiles.title: Stanley K. Hornbeck acknowledgment to G. S. Walden
subfiles.about: Thanks Walden for supplying the text of the company telegram discussed with Hornbeck.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck acknowledges the September 11 letter and the cable they had discussed the previous day. He notes that Walden’s company dispatched the message to London.
